newsitem.title: USA: Burlington Resources buying LL&E for $3 billion.
newsitem.headline: Burlington Resources buying LL&E for $3 billion.

text.p: Burlington Resources Inc. said Thursday it will acquire Louisiana Land & Exploration Co. in a $3 billion stock deal that would form one of the nation's biggest independent oil and natural gas companies.
Under terms of the agreement, a unit of Burlington Resurces will acquire LL&E in an exchange of stock in which LL&E shareholders will receive 1.525 shares of Burlington for each LL&E share they hold.
Burlington will also assume $500 million of LL&E debt.
After the announcement, LL&E's stock shot up as much as $10 in active trading before settling back to trade $8.125 higher at $65.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The companies said that, based on Burlington's closing price of $46.125 on Wednesday, the transaction is worth $3.03 billion, and Burlington is paying around $70 per share, or a 21 percent premium.

But Burlington's stock lost $1.75 to end at $44.375 on the NYSE Thursday as investors fretted that it may be paying too much. Based on that price and its 35.9 million shares outstanding, the transaction is worth $2.93 billion, including the debt.
UBS analyst Michael Barbis said Burlington is paying $8.20 per barrel of oil equivalent for LL&E, which he said is "an expensive price to pay."
"Burlington has obviously factored in a substantial amount of upside associated with Louisiana Land & Exploration's vast Gulf of Mexico acreage position," he said.
Burlington said the deal would lop 10 percent off its earnings per share in 1998, but that cash flow per share -- the measure used for most energy companies -- would rise to $6.60 from $6.35.
However, Burlington Chief Executive Bobby Shackouls, who will head the merged $8.2 billion company, denied he was overpaying.
"We see a lot of value in both of these companies which is not reflected in their share price in the market," he said in an interview.

The Burlington deal is the latest in a series of friendly and hostile transactions in the oil and gas sector that have driven up prices that companies are prepared to pay for each other and properties.
Burlington had long been expected to make an acquisition, and analysts expect many more deals to come.
Shackouls said that with $2.0 billion of financing available, he would not be averse to another deal and would even consider another stock bid if he could find a company like LL&E.

The merged company will have natural gas reserves of 7.7 trillion cubic feet, making it the country's third-largest, and Shackouls said that its size and strong balance sheet would enable it to withstand any price shocks.
"Although there will be some new supply into the market from Canada at the turn of the century, the U.S. has simply not been replacing its reserves," he said.
The companies said they expected the deal to be accounted for as a pooling of interests and to qualify as a tax-free reorganization.
